title: The Lost Boys on Broadway #thelostboys #thelostboysmusical #thelostbo...
transcript: The Lost Boys is either going to be a blockbuster or it'll crash and burn under its operating expenses. I am hoping it's the first case because to me, it has plenty of ingredients that have made hits before — a strong cast, solid material, stunning visuals, wide appeal, and high repeatability. It's based on the 1987 film in which Lucy and her two teenage sons have just moved from Phoenix to Santa Clara, California to get a fresh start, away from her abusive ex-husband. Lucy finds a job, Sam finds some friends, and Michael finds a tribe of vampires. This story works surprisingly well on stage, partially thanks to the seemingly unlimited production budget. From the jump, you know you're getting into an experience, and you know that it's an expensive show just by looking at it. The multi-tiered set design, the visual effects, and the crisp lighting and sound are practically immaculate, but it's not just flashy. The music is great, and the vocal arrangements in particular are hauntingly gorgeous. The cast is full of voices with the range and agility to deliver an ambitious score and tones that can cut straight through a massive theatre like this one — Shoshana Bean is right at home here. The second act feels a little musically bombastic in that almost every song has the heft of a showstopper. For a show that's unapologetically big and maximalist, though, this didn't really bother me. And frankly, I haven't heard a new Broadway score with songs that feel this anthemic in a while, so it's a welcome return. I thought the book was thin and not memorable in a good or bad way, but I was also sitting basically on the moon in an objectively bad seat. Still, I thought the whole experience was both cinematic and immediate, blending the best elements of live performance with transformative visuals. When I go to the theatre, specifically a musical, I usually want to be transported into the world and I want to feel something. I didn't quite feel the latter with this one, but I was certainly transported and amazed in other ways. I also find the show especially impressive in that it didn't do an out of town tryout and it's still in previews today. Putting up a show of this scale must have been a massive undertaking, but at this point it's very well-constructed and well-paced. Director Michael Arden may have earned himself a pair of back to back Tony Awards, sandwiching The Queen of Versailles in an iconically ironic way. Anyway, I would get your tickets to this now before it becomes the next Outsiders. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
reasoning: Creator praises visuals, cast, score, and pacing enthusiastically, and explicitly urges viewers to buy tickets now. Minor caveats about thin book and not feeling emotionally moved keep it from the top of the rave range.
